subject: technology
topic: High-speed internet usage correlates with decreased cognitive control and self-regulation
angle: While excessive internet use is linked to brain changes and deficits in inhibitory control and executive function, the evidence does not establish a causal link between high-speed internet environments and the erosion of neural pathways.
title: The cost of constant connection

hooks.text: Does your internet use affect your focus?
You think you are browsing. Your brain might be reacting.
You are losing the ability to stop.
A thumb moves over a glass screen in a dark room.
Internet use is linked to brain structure changes.

reveal.headline: Problematic internet use is linked to impaired executive functions.
reveal.body: Research shows a link between high levels of internet use and deficits in working memory and inhibition. This is not yet proven as a direct cause.

explain.headline: Your brain patterns change with internet use.
explain.body: Problematic internet use correlates with specific activation in the left middle frontal gyrus and right superior parietal lobule. These areas are involved in inhibitory control tasks.

matters.headline: Your control mechanisms may be weakening.
matters.body: That may be why it feels harder to focus or stop scrolling. Changes in the temporal cortex and ventral striatum are linked to a loss of control over internet use.

example.headline: The late night scroll.
example.body: You sit on your couch at 11 p.m. You intend to check one notification. You find yourself moving from link to link for an hour without a plan.

question.headline: Who is in control of your next click?

claims.text: Brain structure changes in the temporal cortex and ventral striatum are linked to a loss of control over internet use.
claims.quote: Brain structure changes also occur in the temporal cortex and ventral striatum, compromising executive function in planning and reasoning and increasing impulsive risk, resulting in loss of control over internet use.

claims.text: Problematic Usage of the Internet is linked to a neural pattern of increased activation in the left middle frontal gyrus and right superior parietal lobule during inhibitory control tasks.
claims.quote: We conclude that the observed increased activation in the left middle frontal gyrus and right superior parietal lobule during inhibitory control tasks is a neural pattern that is often associated with PUI.

claims.text: Executive functioning problems are linked to academic course performance mediated by studying attention and a single classroom digital metacognition subscale.
claims.quote: Results indicated that executive functioning problems predicted academic course performance mediated by studying attention and a single classroom digital metacognition subscale concerning availability of strategies of when to use mobile phones during lectures.

claims.text: Problematic Internet Use is linked to impairment of executive functions, specifically working memory and inhibition.
claims.quote: the results indicated a good reliability (Cronbach’s α = 0. 810). Additionally, Structural Equation Modelling was performed as a confirmatory factor analysis, revealing that SPIUT scores correlated with executive functions impairment (working memory and inhibition)

claims.text: The use of technology-based interventions provides low-quality evidence for the rehabilitation of executive functions and memory for children and adolescents with TBI.
claims.quote: This review provides low-quality evidence for the use of technology-based interventions in the rehabilitation of executive functions and memory for children and adolescents with TBI.

verdict: The sources show a correlation between problematic internet use and impaired executive functions and specific brain activity patterns, but they do not prove that high-speed internet causes these changes.
caveat: Several studies are observational or provide low-quality evidence, and the meta-analysis on brain activity notes that findings are fragmented and mixed.
caption:
High-speed internet use correlates with changes in how you regulate your behavior.

Research links problematic internet use to impaired executive functions like working memory and inhibition, though a direct causal link is not established. Some findings on brain activity remain fragmented.
